lessons.unit: Spring 1: Programming sequences and online safety
lessons.title: Algorithms: precise steps and spotting mistakes
lessons.bigQuestion: Could a robot make your packed lunch if you only said 'make my lunch'? What would it need to know?
objectives: To understand that an algorithm is a set of precise steps in the right order
successCriteria: All: put the steps of an everyday task in order
Most: write precise steps to move a counter around a grid
Some: find and fix a mistake (bug) in someone else's steps
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: position and direction on a grid
lessons.smsc: Moral: doing a job carefully and in order, like the steps of wudu

keywords.def: a set of steps to do a job, in order
the order the steps go in
exact, so there is only one way to follow it
a mistake in the steps

hook.text: Could a robot make your packed lunch if you only said 'make my lunch'? What would it need to know?
hook.a: It needs every small step, in order, said exactly: that is an algorithm.

starter.q: Which of these is an input device? A) speaker B) keyboard C) screen
Which is an output device? A) mouse B) microphone C) printer
Name one thing you should never share online.
starter.a: For example: your password, home address or school name.

starter.q: What do we call computers joined together so they can share?

teach.heading: What is an algorithm?
bullets: A list of steps to do a job
The steps must be in order
teach.note: Ask: what steps do you follow to make wudu? Order matters. Algorithms are everywhere, not only in computers.

teach.heading: Order matters
bullets: A computer follows the order you give
teach.note: Pupils sort the cards on screen: number each card on their whiteboard.

teach.heading: Be precise
teach.note: Model on a 5 by 5 grid drawn on paper: a counter at the bottom left, a star at the top right.

model.problem: Move the counter from A1 to C3 on the grid.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: Which step is the most precise?
check.why: Only 'forward 3 squares' says exactly how far; the others could be followed many ways.

practice.q: Write the steps to move from A1 to A4 on the grid.
practice.a: Forward 3 squares.
practice.model: Count the squares between A1 and A4: there are 3 moves. Step: forward 3 squares. Test it with your finger.

practice.q: Spot the bug: to reach B2 from A1 Sam wrote 'forward 1, turn left, forward 1'. What is wrong?
practice.a: He should turn right, not left (facing up, B is to the right).

practice.q: Put in order: 'eat', 'wash hands', 'say Bismillah', 'sit down'.
practice.a: Wash hands, sit down, say Bismillah, eat.

independent.q: Core: On your paper grid, write an algorithm to move the counter from A1 to D4. Number each step.
independent.a: For example: forward 3, turn right, forward 3.
independent.model: Teacher writes the first two steps aloud: '1. Forward 3 squares. 2. Turn right.' and checks with a finger on the grid.

independent.q: Extend: Write an algorithm for a grown-up at home to make a cup of water, in at least 5 steps.
independent.a: For example: take a cup, go to the tap, turn the tap on, fill the cup, turn the tap off.

independent.q: Stretch: Write an algorithm with one bug in it. Swap with the screen: can the class find the bug?
independent.a: Any algorithm with one deliberate error, and the fix explained.

exit.q: An algorithm is... A) a computer B) a set of steps in order C) a game
exit.a: B) a set of steps in order
options: A set of steps in order

exit.q: Why must an algorithm be precise?
exit.a: So it can only be followed one way and gives the right result.

lessons.homework: Write the algorithm for one job you do at home (for example tidying your shoes) in 5 numbered steps.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards for the steps and a grid with arrows. EAL: forward, turn, left, right with gestures. Stretch: use the fewest steps possible.

Step cards for 'brushing teeth' (pupil PDF)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Programming sequences and online safety
lessons.title: Scratch: sprites and motion blocks
lessons.bigQuestion: If you tell a ball to 'move 10 steps' twenty times, how far has it gone?
objectives: To understand how motion blocks in Scratch make a sprite move in sequence
successCriteria: All: name the stage, a sprite and a block
Most: join move and turn blocks to make a sprite move
Some: predict where a sprite will end before running the script
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: turns and right angles (90 degrees)

keywords.def: an object on the Scratch stage that we program
the area where sprites move
one instruction you drag into a script
blocks joined together
start the script so it happens

hook.text: If you tell a ball to 'move 10 steps' twenty times, how far has it gone?
hook.a: 200 steps: a computer follows each instruction exactly.

starter.q: What is an algorithm?
starter.a: A set of precise steps in order.

starter.q: A mistake in an algorithm is called a... A) bug B) block C) byte
Is 'go over there' precise?
starter.a: No: it does not say how far or which way.

starter.q: Fix it: 'shoes on, socks on'.

teach.heading: Meet Scratch
bullets: The stage is where things happen
Sprites are the objects we program
teach.note: Share screen. Delete the cat sprite and choose an object sprite (Ball or Rocketship): we program objects, not animals or people.

teach.heading: Motion blocks
teach.note: Show the blue Motion category. Drag 'move 10 steps' and click it. Change 10 to 50.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
go to x: 0 y: 0
move 50 steps
turn right 90 degrees
move 50 steps
code.output: The ball moves right 50 steps, turns, then moves 50 steps down.

teach.heading: Predict, then run
bullets: Say where the sprite will end
teach.note: Predicting first is how programmers check their thinking.

model.problem: Where does the ball end? Start at the centre, facing right.
steps: turn right 90 degrees: now facing down
model.answer: 100 right and 50 down from the centre

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A sprite faces right. It runs 'move 30 steps' three times. How far has it moved?
check.why: Each block runs once, in order: 30 + 30 + 30 = 90.

practice.q: Build: when green flag clicked, move 100 steps. What happens?
practice.a: The sprite moves 100 steps in the way it faces.
practice.model: Teacher drags 'when green flag clicked', then snaps 'move 100 steps' under it, predicts 'right 100', then runs it.

practice.q: Change it so the sprite moves back to where it started.
practice.a: Add 'move -100 steps' or turn 180 degrees and move 100 steps.

practice.q: What does 'go to x: 0 y: 0' do?
practice.a: Sends the sprite to the centre of the stage.

independent.q: Core: Make your sprite move in an L shape: move, turn right 90, move.
independent.a: move 100 steps, turn right 90 degrees, move 50 steps.
independent.model: Teacher builds the first part and predicts aloud before clicking the flag.

independent.q: Extend: Make the sprite trace a square and return to the start.
independent.a: move 100, turn 90, four times (8 blocks).

independent.q: Stretch: Write your script on paper first, predict the end point, then test. Was your prediction right?
independent.a: A written script with a prediction and the result compared.

exit.q: The objects we program in Scratch are called... A) stages B) sprites C) scripts
exit.a: B) sprites

exit.q: Why do we predict before we run a script?
exit.a: To check our thinking and spot bugs before testing.

lessons.homework: Draw (on paper) a 4-block Scratch script that moves a ball in a zig-zag, and write where it will end.
lessons.send: SEND: a printed block card set to arrange before building. EAL: move, turn, run with actions. Stretch: use 'glide 1 secs to x: y:' to make smooth moves.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Programming sequences and online safety
lessons.title: Repeat loops: patterns with fewer blocks
lessons.bigQuestion: Would you rather write 'move, turn' 100 times, or write it once and say 'do this 100 times'?
objectives: To understand how a repeat loop makes a program shorter and easier to read
successCriteria: All: spot the part of a script that repeats
Most: use a repeat block to draw a square
Some: compare a long and a short script and explain which is better
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order and pattern in Islamic geometric art

keywords.def: do the same thing again
blocks that run again and again
something that happens in the same way again
does the job with less work

hook.text: Would you rather write 'move, turn' 100 times, or write it once and say 'do this 100 times'?

starter.q: What is a sprite?
starter.a: An object on the stage that we program.

starter.q: Which block makes a sprite turn? A) move 10 steps B) turn 90 degrees C) when flag clicked
A sprite moves 20 steps 4 times. How far?
Why do we predict before we run?

teach.heading: Spot the repeat
bullets: Look for blocks that come again
teach.note: Show the 8-block square script. Ask pupils to circle the repeating pair on their whiteboard.

teach.heading: The repeat block
teach.note: Pen extension: click Add Extension, choose Pen, then 'pen down' so the sprite draws.

teach.heading: Build a square
teach.note: Model live, then clear the stage with 'erase all'.

model.problem: Draw a square with a loop.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: How many times must we repeat 'move 100, turn 90' to draw a square?
check.why: A square has 4 sides and 4 corners; 90 is the angle, not the count.

practice.q: Draw a square with a repeat block.
practice.a: pen down, repeat 4 (move 100, turn 90).
practice.model: Teacher repeats the model, asking pupils to say each block before it is dragged.

practice.q: Change the loop to draw a bigger square.
practice.a: Change move 100 to move 150.

practice.q: How many blocks did the loop save?
practice.a: The long script had 8 blocks; the loop uses 3, so it saves 5.

independent.q: Core: Draw a row of dashes: repeat 5 (pen down, move 20, pen up, move 20).
independent.a: repeat 5 with pen down, move 20, pen up, move 20 inside.
independent.model: Teacher builds the first dash and shows why 'pen up' leaves a gap.

independent.q: Extend: Draw a triangle. Hint: repeat 3, turn 120.
independent.a: pen down, repeat 3 (move 100, turn 120).

independent.q: Stretch: Put your square loop inside another 'repeat 6' with 'turn 60' to make a pattern. Describe it.
independent.a: Six squares turned around a point make a flower-like pattern.

exit.q: A loop makes a script... A) longer B) shorter and easier to read C) slower
exit.a: B) shorter and easier to read

exit.q: Which part of 'move 50, turn 90, move 50, turn 90, move 50, turn 90, move 50, turn 90' could go in a loop?
exit.a: move 50, turn 90, repeated 4 times.

lessons.homework: Find a repeating pattern at home (tiles, a rug, a fence). Write it as 'repeat __ times: ...'.
lessons.send: SEND: a ready-made script to edit rather than build. EAL: repeat, loop, again. Stretch: draw a hexagon (repeat 6, turn 60).

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Programming with sequence and repetition
lessons.title: Project: an animated greeting card
objectives: Plan a short animation by decomposing it into scenes
Combine events, sequences and loops in one program
Test, debug and improve the program

keywords.def: pictures shown quickly one after another so they seem to move
run a program to check it works
change a program to make it better

starter: Bismillah. What does the 'repeat' block do?
Name two events that can start a Scratch script.
Why do we test our program after each small change?

teach.heading: The project
bullets: Make an animated Eid greeting card.
teach.note: Introduce the project and show a quick example: a star spins while the sprite says 'Eid Mubarak!'. Explain the success criteria and ask pupils to suggest extras. Remember that Eid cards and greetings are a joyful part of our culture.

teach.heading: Plan in parts
teach.note: Reuse decomposition from lesson 1. Pupils sketch three boxes on paper (storyboard) and write which blocks they will need. Check plans before they start building.

teach.heading: Build and test
bullets: Build one scene at a time.
teach.note: Walk round the breakout rooms or watch screens shared in Teams. Ask the question: what did you predict would happen? Highlight good debugging. Typical bugs: loops outside scripts, missing event block, sprite at wrong place.

teach.heading: Share and improve
bullets: Show your card to a partner.
Say one thing that works well.
teach.note: Model kind feedback: 'I like how... Next time you could...'. Link to sincere advice (nasihah) given with kindness. Give time for pupils to make one improvement.

practice: Plan on screen: which blocks would you use to make a star spin forever? (when flag clicked, forever, turn 15 degrees)
Which scene should be built first and why?
Find the bug: the message 'Eid Mubarak!' never appears because the say block is after a forever loop.
independent: Create your animated greeting card with at least 3 scenes, one sequence and one loop.
Test your program three times and write down one bug you fixed.
Present your card to a partner and give one improvement suggestion each.
exit: Name one bug you found and fixed today.
Which part of your program uses a loop?
lessons.homework: Add one more improvement to your card (a new backdrop or a new costume) and describe in one sentence what you changed.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a template project with scenes set up and sentence starters for feedback. Stretch: ask pupils to add a click event so the viewer chooses the next scene.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Programming sequences and online safety
lessons.title: Debugging: find and fix errors
lessons.bigQuestion: A ball should draw a square but it draws a line. Where would you start looking for the mistake?
objectives: To understand how to find and fix a bug by testing a script one step at a time
successCriteria: All: say what a script should do and what it actually does
Most: find the block that causes the bug
Some: fix the bug and test again to prove it works
lessons.smsc: Moral: patience (sabr) and not giving up when something goes wrong

keywords.def: find and fix mistakes in a program
run the program to see if it works
something that goes wrong
change it so it works

hook.text: A ball should draw a square but it draws a line. Where would you start looking for the mistake?

starter.q: How many times do we repeat to draw a square?
What does a loop do?
starter.a: Runs the blocks inside it again and again.

starter.q: Write a loop for a triangle.
Which extension lets a sprite draw?

teach.heading: What is debugging?
bullets: Debugging is finding and fixing it
teach.note: Mistakes are normal. We test, find and fix: this is patience (sabr) in action.

teach.heading: The debugging steps
teach.note: Point to each step as you use it later.

teach.heading: Find the bug
bullets: The script should draw a square
teach.note: Show the buggy script.

code.text:
when green flag clicked
pen down
repeat 4
  move 100 steps
end
turn right 90 degrees
code.output: A straight line: the turn is outside the loop.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Why does the script draw a line?
options: The turn is outside the loop
check.why: The sprite moves 4 times in the same direction, then turns once at the end.

practice.q: Fix the script on the slide so it draws a square.
practice.a: Move 'turn right 90 degrees' inside the repeat, under 'move 100 steps'.
practice.model: Teacher drags the turn block inside the loop, predicts 'a square', then runs it to prove it.

practice.q: Bug: 'repeat 4 (move 100, turn 45)'. What does it draw and how do you fix it?
practice.a: Half of an octagon; change turn 45 to turn 90.

practice.q: Bug: nothing is drawn but the sprite moves. Why?
practice.a: There is no 'pen down' block.

independent.q: Core: Open the class project 'Buggy shapes' and fix the three scripts (square, triangle, dashes).
independent.a: Square: turn inside the loop; triangle: turn 120 not 90; dashes: add pen up.
independent.model: Teacher fixes the square first, saying each debugging step aloud.

independent.q: Extend: Write in the portal response box what each bug was and how you found it. Start: 'The script should... but it...'
independent.a: For example: The script should draw a triangle but it drew part of a square, so I changed turn 90 to turn 120.

independent.q: Stretch: Make a script with one bug for a partner to find in the next lesson.
independent.a: A script with one clear bug and the fix written down.

exit.q: Debugging means... A) deleting the program B) finding and fixing mistakes C) adding more blocks
exit.a: B) finding and fixing mistakes

exit.q: What should you always do after fixing a bug?
exit.a: Test (run) the script again.

lessons.homework: Ask someone at home to follow your square algorithm on paper with one bug in it. Can they find it?
lessons.send: SEND: one bug at a time, with the buggy block highlighted. EAL: bug, fix, test. Stretch: fix a script with two bugs.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Programming sequences and online safety
lessons.title: Powerful passwords
lessons.bigQuestion: Your password is like a key to your house. Who should have a copy?
objectives: To understand what makes a password strong and why we keep it private
successCriteria: All: say who we can share a password with (a trusted adult at home)
Most: tell a strong password from a weak one
Some: make a strong password using three random words
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: keeping safe online and telling a trusted adult

keywords.def: secret words that unlock your account
hard for anyone else to guess
kept to yourself
a grown-up who keeps you safe, like a parent

hook.text: Your password is like a key to your house. Who should have a copy?
hook.a: Only you and your parents: never friends, never strangers online.

islamicLink.text: Keeping a password safe is looking after a trust (amanah). Allah commands us to look after trusts and return them to their owners (an-Nisa 4:58). Our accounts, our devices and our school login are trusts we keep carefully.

starter.q: What is debugging?
starter.a: Finding and fixing mistakes in a program.

starter.q: What should you do after fixing a bug?
What does a loop do?
Name a trusted adult at home.
starter.a: For example: mum, dad, a grandparent who looks after you.

teach.heading: What is a password?
bullets: A secret that unlocks an account
It keeps your work and messages safe
teach.note: Link to their Teams and portal login: they use it every day.

teach.heading: Weak or strong?
bullets: Strong: long and hard to guess
teach.note: Use the sort. Never use your name, birthday or 'password'.

teach.heading: Keep it private
bullets: Never type it for a friend
Never put it in a chat
teach.note: Teams and portal behaviour: never post a password in the class chat; if you think someone knows it, tell your parent and teacher.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A friend in the Teams chat asks for your password to 'help'. What do you do?
options: Say no and tell a trusted adult
check.why: Passwords are never shared, even with friends; a trusted adult can help.

practice.q: Is 'Zayd2018' a strong password? Why?
practice.a: No: it uses a name and a year, which are easy to guess.
practice.model: Teacher thinks aloud: 'Is it long? Quite. Could someone guess it? Yes, it is a name and a birth year. So it is weak.'

practice.q: Make 'catdog' stronger using the three random words rule.
practice.a: For example: CatPencilMountain.

practice.q: Where must a password never be typed in a Teams lesson?
practice.a: In the chat (or anywhere others can see).

independent.q: Core: Write three random words that would make a strong password (do NOT use your real one).
independent.a: For example: TrainLemonCarpet.
independent.model: Teacher picks three things in the room that do not go together: 'Kettle, Moon, Sock: KettleMoonSock.'

independent.q: Extend: Write two rules for keeping a password private in the portal response box. Start: 'I will...'
independent.a: I will only share my password with my parents. I will never type it in the chat.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why 'BlueLampOrange9' is harder to guess than 'blue'.
independent.a: It is longer, uses three unrelated words, capitals and a number, so there are many more possibilities to try.

independent.q: Quiz (portal): 5 questions on password safety.
independent.a: Teacher marks in the portal.

exit.q: Which is the strongest password? A) 123456 B) amina C) TigerSpoonCloud
exit.a: C) TigerSpoonCloud

exit.q: Big question: who should have a copy of your password key?
exit.a: Only me and my parents (trusted adults at home).

lessons.homework: With a parent, check that your school login password is strong and is written only where your parent keeps it safe.
lessons.send: SEND: weak and strong cards with pictures of locks. EAL: strong, weak, private, share. Stretch: explain why websites ask for a number or symbol.

keywords.def: using a computer to design pages with text and pictures
where things are placed on a page
a ready-made layout to fill in
computers joined together to share information

hook.text: A poster and a newspaper both use words and pictures. Why do they look so different?

starter.q: An algorithm is ...
A strong password is ...
Name something you have read today that had pictures and words.

teach.heading: Made with DTP

teach.heading: Sending a document
cycle: To a printer or a friend's computer

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: A big heading, grouped text and one picture

practice.q: Look at the example poster: what is its heading, purpose and audience?
practice.a: Heading: 'Masjid Clean-Up Day'; purpose: invite; audience: families.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: sketch a layout for a poster about our Qur'an club (boxes for heading, text and picture).

independent.model: The teacher sketches the heading box.

independent.q: Extend: choose a template in the DTP tool that fits your sketch.
independent.a: Template chosen.

exit.q: A template is ...
exit.a: a ready-made layout

exit.q: Back to our ponder: A poster and a newspaper both use words and pictures. Why do they look so different?
exit.a: They have different purposes and audiences, so their layouts are different.

the style of letters
the title at the top
line text up left, centre or right

make text flow around an image
